name: Northeast Face Direct

pitch_detail.notes: Muddy rock-and-ice moves off the glacier margin, crossing the moat onto the face.
Steep neve/ice couloir pitch exceeding 50 degrees; rock protection available in the upper section.
Mixed class 3-4 scrambling terrain gaining the face.
The 'Duolith,' a roughly 30-ft rotten granite tower.
Variable line between ascent parties; granite ramps and ledges, including a distinctive offwidth/chimney feature.
Easier scrambling on improved granite to the north ridge and summit.

descent_text: From the summit/north ridge, descend the South Route, class 3-4 scrambling with some rappels and snow traversal to the Spider-Formidable col (crossover saddle), then follow the Ptarmigan Traverse route back across the Middle Cascade Glacier and Red Ledge to the Kool-Aid Lake camp.
approach: Mount Formidable is a deep objective on the Ptarmigan Traverse, reached from the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road. Take the maintained trail to Cascade Pass, then leave it and work across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the far side to camp at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake continue south past Art's Knoll and cross the Red Ledge, then follow a rough path over meadow, snow and talus and drop several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between its two icefalls. Cross the bench to the foot of the Formidable Glacier below the northeast face. Allow a full day or more from the car to Kool-Aid Lake and about three hours from camp to the base of the face. The descent is the South Route, back over the Spider-Formidable col and across the Middle Cascade Glacier and Red Ledge to camp. This is a multi-day glaciated objective that needs glacier travel skills.
overview: Rarely-repeated alpine rock route on Mount Formidable's northeast face above the heavily crevassed Formidable Glacier in the North Cascades; first climbed in 2002, with a documented second ascent not until 2013.
beta: Lower pitches climb a rubble-covered class 4 gully into a snow couloir that steepens past 65 degrees with overhanging chalkstones near its top; the crux is two 5.6 pitches around the 'duolith,' a loose 30-foot granite tower split by a 3-foot crack, climbed on sparse protection (one 80-meter pitch protected by a single piece) before easier class 3-4 terrain leads up the north ridge crest to the summit.
fa: Jens Klubberud and Loren Campbell, July 20, 2002
